proof:
# Fixed-sector Lorentz-row maxima, singular-block rigidity, and the cap-band pentagon reduction

This is an ordinary planar theorem about three concurrent lines. It is a new optimization consequence of the exact sector PSD criterion. It does not preserve neighboring mixed-integer fibers, and does not assert the Lorentz inequality for arbitrary bodies.

## 1. Data, objective, and attained maxima

Use the six cyclic ray endpoints

    P=( (A,0), (0,B), (-t,t), (-a,0), (0,-b), (r,-r) ),
    R=(A,B,t,a,b,r),

with all radii positive. Fix six positive sector areas W_0,...,W_5, and assume that at least one convex body containing zero in its interior realizes these data for some radii. Indices of rays and sectors are cyclic modulo six. The three cap areas and coarea-normalized central chord lengths are

    q_1=W_0+W_4+W_5,       ell_1=B+b,
    q_2=W_0+W_1+W_2,       ell_2=A+a,
    q_3=W_2+W_3+W_4,       ell_3=t+r.

Put k=sum W_i and

    M=sum_(j=1)^3 q_j/ell_j,
    f_j=2 sqrt(k q_j)/(ell_j M),
    Phi_i=f_i+(f_j+f_l)^2/4,       {i,j,l}={1,2,3}.

Thus k and every q_j are fixed as radii vary. Any additional restriction depending only on the six sector areas is preserved by all variations below.

Set c_i=1/(2W_i). The exact feasibility theorem says that the core constraints

    R_i R_(i+1)<=2W_i

and positive semidefiniteness of the symmetric matrix

    L_ii=c_(i-1)+c_i-1/R_i^2,
    L_(i,i+1)=c_i-1/(R_i R_(i+1))

are necessary and sufficient for actual convex-body realization; all other off-diagonal entries vanish. A core sector means equality in its core constraint. Equivalently its excess parameter h_i=1/(R_i R_(i+1))-c_i is zero. This criterion, including realization and boundary cases, was proved in `candidate 2e26c63010f03ffc`.

The feasible radius set is compact in the positive orthant. Indeed, its diagonal inequalities imply

    R_i>=1/sqrt(c_(i-1)+c_i)=:l_i>0,

and its core inequalities then imply R_i<=2W_i/l_(i+1). Within this positive compact box all the constraints are closed. Consequently every Phi_i attains a maximum over actual feasible data. No compactness of a selected polygonal reconstruction is required.

**Theorem.** At any local maximum of Phi_i in this fixed-sector feasible radius set:

1. L is singular.
2. At least two sectors are cores. More precisely, if the three derivatives with respect to the chord lengths are not all zero, then some chord with positive derivative has a core adjacent to each of its two endpoints. If all three derivatives vanish, every one of the six endpoints is adjacent to a core, so there are at least three cores.
3. If exactly two sectors are cores, both connected blocks of L are singular. Every actual body realizing the maximizing data is the same unique quadrilateral, with its four vertices in the four positive-excess sectors.
4. More generally, L has at least two singular connected blocks. If all three cap fractions are at most 128/279, a maximizing realization with at most five vertices exists. Sections 12–13 prove these stronger conclusions and specify the remaining graph types.

All statements concern local maxima in the finite radius data. An attained global maximum suffices. No claim about an arbitrary Hausdorff-local maximum of one body is needed.

## 2. Convexity in one projective inverse-chord coordinate

Write x_j=1/ell_j and r_j=sqrt(q_j/k)>0. The projective weights

    z_j=q_j x_j / sum_l q_l x_l

are positive and sum to one, and f_j=2z_j/r_j. Keep two inverse chords fixed and vary x_s>0. Set

    tau=q_s x_s/(q_s x_s+C),       C=sum_(j!=s) q_j x_j>0.

Then tau increases strictly with x_s, z_s=tau, and z_j=(1-tau) zbar_j for j!=s, with positive fixed zbar_j summing to one.

If s=i, the selected row is

    Phi_i(tau)=2tau/r_i + D(1-tau)^2,
    D=(sum_(j!=i) zbar_j/r_j)^2>0.

This is strictly convex. If s!=i and l is the remaining index, then

    Phi_i(tau)=2zbar_i(1-tau)/r_i
                  +[tau/r_s+(1-tau)zbar_l/r_l]^2.

This is convex. If its quadratic coefficient vanishes, its derivative is the strictly negative constant -2zbar_i/r_i. Therefore, in EVERY coordinate, a zero first derivative implies strictly positive quadratic curvature in tau.

Two consequences will be used repeatedly:

* If partial Phi_i/partial x_s<0, decreasing x_s strictly increases Phi_i throughout the interval to its left. This follows because the derivative of the convex polynomial is then negative everywhere to the left.
* If that partial derivative is zero, either direction of a nonzero sufficiently small change in x_s strictly increases Phi_i, by the strictly positive quadratic coefficient.

No assertion of Euclidean convexity in the untransformed radius coordinates is made.

## 3. Feasible radius increases and the core conclusion

Increasing one radius R_s while keeping the areas and all other radii fixed preserves feasibility up to the finite bound

    R_s'<=min{2W_(s-1)/R_(s-1), 2W_s/R_(s+1)}.

For completeness, every changed entry of L increases, and the displayed core bounds keep all its off-diagonal entries nonpositive. For every real vector v,

    v^T L' v >= |v|^T L' |v| >= |v|^T L |v| >=0.

The exact PSD theorem realizes the changed data. This includes the finite closed upper bound. It is the radius-monotonicity mechanism proved in `candidate 83b3822a403eee2c`.

Let d_j=partial Phi_i/partial ell_j at a maximum. These derivatives exist because all raw quantities are positive. The objective is homogeneous of degree zero in the three chord lengths, so

    ell_1 d_1+ell_2 d_2+ell_3 d_3=0.                 (1)

Also partial Phi_i/partial x_j=-ell_j^2 d_j.

If d_j>0, increasing either endpoint radius of chord j decreases x_j and strictly increases Phi_i by Section 2, unless that endpoint is already at its core bound. Thus BOTH endpoints of this chord must be adjacent to a core. A single sector cannot be adjacent to opposite endpoints, so at least two cores are required.

If the d_j are not all zero, (1) supplies at least one positive d_j. If all d_j vanish, Section 2 shows that increasing ANY radius with room before its core bound strictly increases Phi_i. Hence every endpoint must already be adjacent to a core. Each core touches only two endpoints, requiring at least three cores. This proves conclusion 2.

The derivative signs can also be read directly from the actual row data. Put F=f_i, g=f_j+f_l and H=F+g^2/2=2Phi_i-F. Direct differentiation gives

    partial Phi_i/partial x_i=(q_i/M)(2/r_i-H),
    partial Phi_i/partial x_j=(q_j/M)(g/r_j-H),     j!=i,

Here x_s=1/ell_s, as in Section 2. Thus the core requirement applies to the selected chord whenever H>=2/r_i, and to a nonselected chord j whenever H>=g/r_j. Equality still requires both endpoint core bounds: its one-coordinate second derivative in tau is strictly positive. These tests make the finite stratum selection explicit; they are not additional assumptions.

## 4. Positive definiteness is impossible

Suppose L were positive definite. Decreasing any single radius slightly preserves positive definiteness by openness and improves both adjacent core inequalities. Thus that decrease is feasible.

If the d_j are not all zero, equation (1) supplies a negative d_j. Decreasing an endpoint radius of that chord raises Phi_i to first order. If all d_j vanish, the same decrease strictly raises Phi_i by the one-coordinate quadratic argument in Section 2. Both contradict local maximality. Hence L is singular, proving conclusion 1.

This argument permits core equalities; it does not require all sector excesses to be positive.

## 5. Exactly two cores force both blocks to be singular

Assume there are exactly two cores. Section 3 rules out all d_j=0. Choose a chord with positive derivative and relabel the cyclic endpoint indices so it is the chord ell_1=B+b, with d_1>0. This is only a relabeling of the three chords and six cyclic nodes; the one-coordinate proof above applies to any selected row and any coordinate. The two cores must be one adjacent to node 1 and one adjacent to node 4. Their edge pairs are

    (0,3), (0,4), (1,3), (1,4).

All other h_s are strictly positive, and deleting the two zero edges splits L into two connected path blocks.

A basic allowed operation used below is this: decrease a boundary radius in one block and increase the adjacent radius in the other block so that their shared core product stays constant. If the decreased-radius block is positive definite, it remains so for small changes. In the other block every changed matrix entry increases, and its strict internal excess keeps the Z signs. Hence that block remains PSD by the absolute-value argument. The other core product stays fixed. All other core inequalities either improve or retain their strict slack. Therefore the operation is genuinely feasible by the exact criterion.

### Cores 0 and 4

The short block is {5,0}, and the long block is {1,2,3,4}.

If the long block were positive definite, either internal radius t=R_2 or a=R_3 could vary slightly in BOTH directions while the other block stayed fixed. Their adjacent excesses are strict. Local maximality therefore forces d_3=d_2=0, contradicting (1) and d_1>0. Thus the long block is singular.

If the short block were positive definite, perform the two allowed operations separately. Decreasing A and increasing B with AB fixed has first variation B d_1-A d_2, using the exponential parametrization A(epsilon)=A exp(-epsilon), B(epsilon)=B exp(epsilon). Local maximality would require A d_2>=B d_1>0. Decreasing r and increasing b with rb fixed similarly requires r d_3>=b d_1>0. These two inequalities make all three d_j positive, contradicting (1). Hence the short block is singular too.

### Cores 1 and 3

The short block is {2,3}, and the long block is {4,5,0,1}. Positive definiteness of the long block permits both-way changes of r and A, again forcing d_3=d_2=0 and contradicting (1).

If the short block were positive definite, the operations t down with B up (Bt fixed), and a down with b up (ab fixed), would respectively require t d_3>=B d_1>0 and a d_2>=b d_1>0. This contradicts (1). Both blocks are singular.

### Cores 0 and 3

The blocks are {1,2,3} and {4,5,0}. If the first were positive definite, its internal radius t could vary in both directions, forcing d_3=0. Equation (1) then gives d_2<0. The allowed operation a down and b up, with ab fixed, has strictly positive first variation b d_1-a d_2, a contradiction.

If the second block were positive definite, its internal radius r likewise gives d_3=0 and d_2<0. The operation A down and B up, with AB fixed, has positive first variation. Thus both blocks are singular.

### Cores 1 and 4

The blocks are {2,3,4} and {5,0,1}. Positive definiteness of either block forces d_2=0 by varying its internal radius a or A. Equation (1) then gives d_3<0. In the first case use t down and B up with Bt fixed; in the second use r down and b up with rb fixed. Each has positive first variation and gives a contradiction. Both blocks are singular here as well.

This exhausts the four patterns, including all possible derivative sign patterns consistent with (1). In particular it does not assume the monotonicity pattern of an inverse-chord-weight objective.

## 6. Actual quadrilateral rigidity

A singular connected symmetric PSD block whose internal off-diagonal entries are strictly negative has a strictly positive null vector. Indeed a least Rayleigh minimizer exists on the unit sphere; replacing it by its absolute value cannot increase the quadratic form. A zero coordinate of the resulting nonnegative null vector forces both neighbors to vanish, and connectivity would force the whole vector to be zero. Concatenate the two positive block null vectors to obtain w>0 with Lw=0.

Here are the exact rigidity consequences, including arbitrary curved realizing bodies. The exact sector reconstruction has harmonic edge charges r_s,s_s, zero on core edges, and nonnegative node slacks delta_s, with Gram identity

    v^T L v=sum_s delta_s v_s^2
        +sum_(h_s>0) (s_s v_s-r_s v_(s+1))^2/(r_s+s_s).

At v=w every term vanishes. Thus all node slacks are zero, and the charge ratio on each positive edge is fixed by w. The harmonic identity r_s s_s/(r_s+s_s)=h_s fixes both charges. Scaling a block's null vector changes none of its edge ratios. Each inserted positive-excess sector vertex is therefore uniquely fixed. A core sector contributes just the straight segment between its prescribed endpoints.

Zero node slack makes the two boundary segments adjacent to every prescribed endpoint collinear. Hence every prescribed endpoint lies in the relative interior of an edge of the replacement polygon. Each positive-excess inserted vertex is a strict turn, while a core sector has no new vertex. There are exactly four positive-excess sectors, so the unique replacement is a quadrilateral.

For an arbitrary actual realizing body K, choose an actual supporting line at every prescribed endpoint. The support-preserving sector replacement has the same data and must equal this unique quadrilateral P. Every retained endpoint lies in the relative interior of an edge of P, so its supporting line is uniquely that edge line. These lines include all four edge lines of P; thus K is contained in P. Their areas both equal sum W_s. Proper inclusion of compact full-dimensional convex bodies would give a positive-area difference, so K=P. This proves conclusion 3 for every actual realizing body.

The support-preserving reconstruction and Gram identity are established in the exact-sector sources; the same boundary-aware rigidity argument is also recorded in `candidate 50872e565640d12b`.

## 7. What this reduction does and does not establish

For any actual planar body with these fixed lines, maximize a selected Phi_i over its six fixed sector areas. A maximizing datum exists. It has singular L and at least two core sectors. If there are exactly two cores, the maximum is attained by an actual unique quadrilateral. Cases with three or more cores remain, as does the row inequality for the resulting quadrilaterals.

Therefore a hypothetical general-body Lorentz failure can be moved, without decreasing its selected row and without changing any fixed-line cap/profile data, to either this genuine quadrilateral stratum or a stratum with at least three cores. No conclusion that all maxima are triangles is made. The already proved full local triangle neighborhood excludes nearby failures, but it does not by itself eliminate either remaining global stratum.

## 8. The remaining core strata have a maximizing polygon with at most seven vertices

There is a further rank restriction at any fixed-sector local maximum: every positive-definite connected block of L has at most TWO nodes.

Indeed, a connected block with at least three nodes has an internal node s. Both adjacent h values are strictly positive. If the block were positive definite, the radius R_s could vary slightly in both directions: the block remains PD by continuity, the two core constraints retain their strict slack, and every other block remains unchanged. If the corresponding chord derivative is nonzero, one direction increases Phi_i. If it is zero, Section 2's strictly positive one-coordinate curvature increases Phi_i in either direction. Both contradict maximality. Thus all connected blocks with at least three nodes are singular.

To turn this into an actual vertex count, use the direct least-eigenvector reconstruction from Section 7 of the PSD source. In each connected block choose its positive least eigenvector w. Its least eigenvalue is zero for a singular block and strictly positive for a PD block. The reconstructed harmonic charges have node slack

    delta_s=(Lw)_s/w_s,

so delta_s=0 at every node in a singular block and delta_s>0 at every node in a PD block. Consequently the prescribed ray endpoint is a strict polygon vertex precisely at a PD-block node; at a singular-block node it is a relative-interior point of a straight polygon edge. Each positive-excess sector contributes one additional strict vertex. Zero-excess sectors contribute none. The resulting actual realizing polygon therefore has exactly

    p+v_PD                                                   (2)

vertices, where p is the number of positive edges h_s>0 and v_PD is the number of nodes in PD blocks. This assertion concerns this specified reconstruction; no uniqueness of a body with a PD block is claimed.

If there are exactly two cores, Section 5 makes every block singular and (2) gives the already proved quadrilateral. If there are at least three cores, p<=3. Since L is singular, at least one block is singular. The following finite enumeration bounds (2); path lengths below count positive edges.

* p=3 with one length-3 path: its four-node block is singular, so v_PD<=2 and p+v_PD<=5.
* p=3 with paths of lengths 2 and 1: the three-node block is singular, so v_PD<=3 and p+v_PD<=6.
* p=3 with three length-1 paths: there are three two-node blocks; at least one is singular, so v_PD<=4 and p+v_PD<=7.
* p=2 with one length-2 path: its three-node block is singular, so v_PD<=3 and p+v_PD<=5.
* p=2 with two length-1 paths: the remaining blocks are singletons; at least one node belongs to a singular block, so v_PD<=5 and p+v_PD<=7.
* p=1: at least one node belongs to a singular block, so p+v_PD<=6.
* p=0: at least one singleton block is singular, so p+v_PD<=5.

These are all subgraphs of the six-cycle with at most three positive edges. Hence every fixed-sector maximum of a selected row has an actual polygonal realization with at most seven vertices.

**Finite global reduction.** If any ordinary planar convex body violates a selected generalized Lorentz row, a body with at most seven vertices also violates that same row, has exactly the same three fixed-line cap areas and total area, and can be chosen at a fixed-sector global row maximum. If the maximizing data have exactly two cores, this replacement is the unique quadrilateral of Section 6. Otherwise it belongs to one of the explicitly listed at-least-three-core strata. Fixed-line cap ceilings and sorted cap-profile inequalities are preserved exactly.

This reduction supplies a finite ordinary geometric target. It does not prove the row inequality for these polygons, does not show that all maximizers are triangles or quadrilaterals, and does not preserve mixed-fiber compatibility.

## 9. A sharper reduction to six vertices, with two explicit hexagon strata

The seven-vertex bound can be sharpened using the entire positive-definite principal submatrix, even when it consists of several separate blocks.

### The only singular block cannot be a singleton

Suppose node s is the only singular block and is a singleton. The principal submatrix on the other five nodes is positive definite. Each of the three nodes s+2,s+3,s+4 can be decreased slightly without changing the singular row or column: none is adjacent to s. All its core products decrease, and the five-node principal submatrix remains PD by openness, including any newly nonzero entries at former zero edges within that submatrix. Hence each of these radius decreases is feasible.

At a local row maximum, its chord derivative must be strictly positive. A negative derivative would give a positive first-order gain on decreasing the radius; a zero derivative would give a strict second-order gain by Section 2. The three consecutive nodes represent all three different chords. Thus all three d_j would be positive, contradicting (1). This excludes the stated singular-block pattern.

### The only singular block cannot have two nodes

Relabel cyclic indices so the singular block is {1,2}. Its internal edge h_1 is positive, and its two boundary edges h_0,h_2 vanish. The principal submatrix on the other four nodes {3,4,5,0} is positive definite, whether or not it has internal zero edges.

Nodes 4 and 5 have no neighbor in the singular block, so each radius can be decreased slightly while leaving the singular block uncoupled. The same argument as above gives d_1>0 and d_3>0. Homogeneity then implies d_2<0.

Now decrease A=R_0 and increase B=R_1 so AB stays constant. On the four-node PD principal submatrix this is a continuous sufficiently small perturbation. On the singular two-node block the entries affected by B increase; its positive internal excess remains strict for a small change, so it stays a PSD Z-matrix. The separating edge 0 remains zero, and the other separating edge 2 is unchanged. Every other core inequality either improves or stays unchanged. Thus the actual data remain feasible. The first variation is

    B d_1-A d_2>0,

a contradiction. This excludes a unique singular block of size two.

### Adjacent singular singleton blocks are impossible

This last observation is geometric and does not use maximality. A singular singleton at node s has zero node slack and both adjacent sectors are cores. Consequently P_(s-1),P_s,P_(s+1) are collinear. If the next singleton s+1 were also singular, P_s,P_(s+1),P_(s+2) would be collinear too. The four consecutive prescribed endpoints would lie on one line. Their first and last endpoints are opposite rays, so that line passes through zero. This contradicts that zero is an interior point of the realizing body and the intermediate ray points are nonzero. Thus two singular singleton blocks cannot be adjacent.

### Complete surviving count

Return to the enumeration in Section 8. For p=3 with three two-node blocks, seven vertices would require exactly one singular two-node block; this has just been excluded. For p=2 with two length-1 paths, seven vertices would require exactly one singular singleton; this too is excluded. The cases p=1 and p=0 similarly improve because their largest counts would require a unique singular singleton. It follows that every fixed-sector row maximum has a polygonal realization with at most SIX vertices.

Moreover the only ways the specified least-eigenvector reconstruction can have exactly six vertices are:

**Hexagon type A.** There are three positive edges, split into a length-2 path and a length-1 path. The three-node block is singular, the two-node block is positive definite, and the remaining singleton is positive definite. It is the unique-singular-block pattern with singular block size three.

**Hexagon type B.** There are two positive edges, forming two two-node positive-definite blocks. Both remaining singleton blocks are singular. These singletons cannot be adjacent by the preceding argument, so they are opposite in the six-cycle; equivalently the two positive edges are opposite.

Every other maximizing graph has a realizing polygon with at most five vertices, except that exactly two core edges already give the stronger unique-quadrilateral conclusion. The two hexagon types are not claimed to be attained or to violate any row inequality; they are the complete remaining graph possibilities at this level of the argument.

Consequently, any hypothetical ordinary-body violation of a selected generalized Lorentz row can be replaced, preserving all six sector areas and all fixed-line cap/profile constraints, by a violation on a polygon with at most six vertices. In the six-vertex case it can be taken in one of the two explicitly described singular/PD graph strata. This is a sharper finite geometric target, not a proof of the target inequality.

## 10. An exact two-variable area region for hexagon type B

This section parameterizes type B as actual bodies, rather than formal independent cap data. Place its opposite singular singleton nodes at P_0=(A,0) and P_3=(-a,0). The four core sectors are W_0,W_2,W_3,W_5. Their zero singleton slacks give

    A=Br/(B+r),          a=bt/(b+t).                       (3)

Conversely choose ANY B,b,r,t>0, define A,a by (3), and prescribe

    W_0=AB/2,  W_2=at/2,  W_3=ab/2,  W_5=Ar/2,
    W_1=X,     W_4=Y.

The core lower bounds are X>=Bt/2 and Y>=br/2. These data have an actual convex-body realization if and only if the following further condition holds:

    br>Bt:  X <= Bt(bt+Br+2br) / [2(br-Bt)],
    br<Bt:  Y <= br(bt+Br+2Bt) / [2(Bt-br)],
    br=Bt:  no further bound.                            (4)

In each of the first two cases the other area is unbounded above. All equalities in these conditions are included. This is an exact realization statement, not an extrapolation from numerical data.

To prove it, the two singleton blocks vanish identically by (3). Put

    alpha=1/(Br), beta=1/(bt), u=1/(2X), v=1/(2Y).

The remaining two blocks are exactly

    L_X = [[u+alpha, u-1/(Bt)],
           [u-1/(Bt), u+beta]],

    L_Y = [[v+beta, v-1/(br)],
           [v-1/(br), v+alpha]].

All diagonal entries are strictly positive. Their determinants are

    det L_X = u[alpha+beta+2/(Bt)] + alpha beta -1/(Bt)^2,
    det L_Y = v[alpha+beta+2/(br)] + alpha beta -1/(br)^2.

Thus the PSD conditions are linear in u,v. If br>Bt only the X condition is restrictive, and solving it gives precisely the first line of (4). If br<Bt the Y condition gives the second line. Equality of br and Bt makes both determinants strictly positive for every finite positive X,Y. The core conditions supply the Z signs. The exact PSD theorem now proves both necessity and sufficiency, with all boundary cases tracked.

If both core inequalities are strict and the finite inequality in (4), when present, is also strict, the two nontrivial blocks are positive definite. The least-eigenvector reconstruction is an actual hexagon: its vertices are P_1,P_2,P_4,P_5 and one inserted vertex in each of sectors 1 and 4. The other two prescribed ray points P_0,P_3 lie strictly inside its two opposite straight boundary edges. At a finite bound in (4), the corresponding two-node block becomes singular and its two prescribed ray vertices disappear; that reconstruction is a quadrilateral. At a core lower bound the corresponding inserted vertex disappears. No smaller polygon or arbitrary triangle is substituted in the interior regime.

All cap/chord data needed for a row inequality are now explicit:

    k = X+Y+[AB+at+ab+Ar]/2,
    q_1 = Y+[AB+Ar]/2,
    q_2 = X+[AB+at]/2,
    q_3 = Y+[at+ab]/2,
    ell_1=B+b, ell_2=Br/(B+r)+bt/(b+t), ell_3=r+t.

They must be inserted together into the definition of Phi_i. Conditions on cap fractions or the sorted cap profile remain exact inequalities in this same four-radius/two-area family. Formula (4) does not prove those resulting row inequalities; it supplies a complete actual geometric feasible region for one of the two surviving hexagon strata.

## 11. Actual type-B hexagons can have all three caps below one half

The hypothesis that all three cap fractions are strictly below 1/2 does NOT eliminate type B. The following exact rational body is a certificate, not a numerical screen.

Take B=t=1, b=r=11/10 and hence A=a=11/21. Choose

    X=63/100,       Y=61/100.

Both core inequalities are strict: X>1/2 and Y>121/200. Here br>Bt and the finite upper bound on X in (4) is 11, so both nontrivial blocks are positive definite. An explicit realizing hexagon, in cyclic order, has vertices

    (0,1), (-63/100,63/50), (-1,1),
    (0,-11/10), (61/110,-61/55), (11/10,-11/10).

The two inserted vertices are obtained with equal positive sector coefficients: X/(Bt)=63/100 in sector 1, and Y/(br)=61/121 in sector 4. The other two ray points (11/21,0),(-11/21,0) lie in the relative interiors of the two retained straight edges. The exact PSD reconstruction proves strict convexity and the specified ray/sector data; alternatively they follow directly by determinants and line intersections of the printed vertices.

The exact total and cap areas are

    k=117/50,
    q_1=q_3=29/25,
    q_2=2423/2100.

Consequently q_1/k=q_3/k=58/117<1/2 and q_2/k=2423/4914<1/2. This disproves the proposed half-cap exclusion using an actual convex body, rather than a formal PSD array.

This example does NOT meet the stronger ceiling 128/279 and does NOT satisfy the sorted cap-profile bound. Its sorted profile excess is

    q_min+q_mid+q_max/4-k=277/1050>0.

No Lorentz-row violation, mixed-fiber compatibility, or criticality is asserted for the example. It only shows that the strict half-cap condition alone is insufficient to eliminate type B.

## 12. At least two singular blocks: type A is impossible at a row maximum

In fact EVERY fixed-sector local row maximum has at least two singular connected blocks of L. Sections 9 already exclude a unique singular block of size one or two. Exactly two cores force both blocks singular by Section 5. With at least three cores, there are at most three positive edges, so every connected block has at most four nodes. It remains only to exclude a unique singular block with three or four nodes.

### A unique singular three-node block

Relabel its nodes as {0,1,2}; the principal submatrix on {3,4,5} is positive definite. Both positive edges adjacent to the internal node 1 are strict. Increasing R_1=B alone is feasible by radius monotonicity, so maximality and Section 2 imply

    d_1<0.

Here equality is excluded by strictly positive projective curvature, not merely by a first-order argument.

On the other hand the opposite radius R_4=b has both its neighbors in the PD principal complement. It can be decreased slightly without changing or coupling to the singular block; every affected core product decreases and the PD principal submatrix remains PD by continuity. Thus maximality implies d_1>0, again with equality excluded by curvature. This is a contradiction. In particular hexagon type A from Section 9 never occurs at a row maximum, irrespective of cap ceilings or profile assumptions.

### A unique singular four-node block

Such a block can be relabeled {0,1,2,3}. Its three internal edges are positive; because there are at least three cores, all remaining edges 3,4,5 are cores. Its complement {4,5} is a positive-definite principal submatrix (in this pattern its two nodes are singleton blocks).

Both internal singular-block radii B=R_1 and t=R_2 can be increased alone. Maximality therefore forces d_1<0 and d_3<0. Homogeneity (1) then gives d_2>0.

Make the simultaneous variation

    A(epsilon)=A exp(epsilon),   a(epsilon)=a exp(epsilon),
    r(epsilon)=r exp(-epsilon),  b(epsilon)=b exp(-epsilon),

with B,t fixed and epsilon>0 small. The two separating core products Ar and ab remain exactly fixed. The third core product br decreases. The singular four-node block changes entrywise upward and retains its Z signs, since its internal excesses are strict; hence it remains PSD. The two-node PD principal complement changes continuously, including a new negative off-diagonal entry at its former core edge, and remains PD for sufficiently small epsilon. Thus the full actual data remain feasible.

The objective's first variation is

    (A+a)d_2-b d_1-r d_3>0,

a contradiction. A unique singular four-node block is impossible as well.

This completes the proof that the number of singular connected blocks is at least two. Equivalently, the matrix nullity is at least two, since every connected singular Z-matrix block here has a one-dimensional positive kernel.

## 13. The cap-band problem reduces to actual pentagons

Combine Section 12 with the positive-edge enumeration. At a fixed-sector row maximum:

* Four positive edges (exactly two cores) give the unique quadrilateral of Section 6.
* Three positive edges in one length-3 path give a singular four-node block and at least one further singular singleton, so p+v_PD<=4.
* Three positive edges in paths of lengths 2 and 1 give a singular three-node block and another singular block. The only way to have five vertices is a singular singleton and a PD two-node block; otherwise there are at most four.
* Three isolated positive edges require at least two singular two-node blocks. There are at most five vertices, with equality only if the third two-node block is PD.
* Two positive edges in one length-2 path give a singular three-node block and at least one singular singleton, hence at most four vertices.
* Two isolated positive edges give at most five vertices unless BOTH singleton blocks are singular and both two-node blocks are PD. The latter is precisely hexagon type B.
* One positive edge gives at most five vertices; equality requires its two-node block to be PD and exactly two of the four singleton blocks to be singular.
* No positive edges give at most four vertices, since at least two singleton blocks are singular.

The already independently audited theorem `candidate 10ff75afdda8a25f` proves that every actual type-B body, including its boundary strata, has a cap fraction at least 8/17. Its proof retains the actual four core sectors and the two opposite collinearities and does not assume any row inequality. Therefore it excludes type B whenever all three original cap fractions are strictly below 8/17, in particular when they are at most 128/279.

**Pentagon reduction theorem.** For three fixed balanced spanning planar normals and an interior source, let an actual convex body have q_i/k<=128/279 for all i. For each selected row Phi_i, there is an actual polygon with at most five vertices, the same six sector areas and hence the same total area, cap fractions and sorted cap profile, whose selected row is at least as large. It may be chosen at a fixed-sector global row maximum. The corresponding PSD matrix has at least two singular connected blocks. The transformation is ordinary and does not preserve neighboring mixed fibers.

To prove the statement, pass to the fixed canonical normals, hold the actual six sector areas fixed, and take an attained row maximum from Section 1. Every cap fraction is preserved, excluding type B. The above enumeration and the explicit least-eigenvector reconstruction produce the asserted polygon. Mapping back preserves the rows and every stated area ratio.

For clarity, the only possible five-vertex reconstruction graphs have the following block-size/sign patterns, with singular denoted S and positive definite denoted D:

    three positive edges: (3S,2D,1S) or (2S,2S,2D);
    two positive edges:   (2S,2D,1S,1D);
    one positive edge:    (2D,1S,1S,1D,1D).

In the last pattern the singular singleton nodes cannot be adjacent. These are necessary graph types, not assertions of realizability, equality, or a row violation. Every remaining row maximum has a polygonal realization with at most four vertices.

The ordinary generalized Lorentz inequality remains to be proved or disproved on these actual pentagon/quadrilateral strata. The full local triangle neighborhood controls nearby bodies, but no global triangle-extremizer conclusion is inferred from it.
